refnamediv.refpurpose: Enroll certificates into the kernel's trust keyrings at boot

refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: systemd-keyring-setup.service is an early boot service that populates the kernel's dedicated trust keyrings with X.509 certificates found in the File Hierarchy for the Verification of OS Artifacts (VOA), and then seals the keyrings so that the set of trusted certificates cannot be changed anymore for the lifetime of the kernel. This allows the kernel to authenticate signatures with keys shipped by the OS vendor or configured by the administrator, without rebuilding the kernel or enrolling keys into the firmware.
The following keyrings are provisioned, each from a VOA role of the same trust domain:

row.entry: Signatures on the root hash of dm-verity volumes, such as those of Discoverable Disk Images set up by systemd-veritysetup@.service8, systemd-dissect1 or the RootImage= setting of services
Built-in signatures of fs-verity protected files

refsect1.para: For each keyring the certificates below /etc/voa/, /run/voa/, /usr/local/share/voa/ and /usr/share/voa/ are looked up as OS/ROLE/default/x509/*-certificate.pem and OS/trust-anchor-ROLE/default/x509/*-certificate.pem. Both artifact verifiers and trust anchors end up in the same keyring, as the kernel validates certificate chains itself. Every copy of a certificate in every load path counts, and a certificate whose file name is masked via a symlink to /dev/null in any load path is ignored in all of them. Only the first certificate of a file is used. Symlinks are followed only within the hierarchy, to a load path of the same or lower priority, to a target of the same name, and never into /run/voa/. The OS identifiers looked up are derived from os-release5: the exact identifier composed of the ID=, VERSION_ID=, VARIANT_ID=, IMAGE_ID= and IMAGE_VERSION= fields, and the bare ID=. Both directories are searched. The fs-verity and bpf roles are defined by systemd, the image role by the specification.

The .dm-verity and .bpf keyrings are sealed empty by the kernel unless dm_verity.keyring_unsealed=1 respectively bpf.keyring_unsealed=1 is passed on the kernel command line, and the kernel only consults them once they hold at least one key and have been sealed again. The service therefore enrolls the certificates and seals the keyring in one go, before the first verity volume is set up, and it seals these two keyrings even if no certificate was found, so that nothing running later in the boot can provision them instead. The .fs-verity keyring is never sealed by the kernel and is consulted whenever it holds a key; it is sealed once it holds at least one key, and left open otherwise so that a later boot stage may still populate it.

Sealing a keyring stops further keys from being added, but not from being removed. Hence the service also drops all permissions on the keyring afterwards, except for the search permission the kernel itself uses and the owner's view permission. This makes the enrolled set immutable for the lifetime of the kernel, even for the root user, who may still see the keyring and its keys in /proc/keys, but neither list, change nor unlock it. This is also how a later boot stage — the host system after the initrd, or the next boot of a soft-rebooted kernel — recognizes that the keyring was provisioned already.

The service runs in the initrd and in the host system, and the initrd is where provisioning is expected to happen: the root file system may itself be a signed dm-verity volume, and the keyring must be complete before it is set up. Consequently the initrd has to carry the certificates, the dm-verity kernel module, and this service. On the host system the service finds the keyrings sealed and locked down, and does nothing.

refsect1.title: Credentials
refsect1.para: Certificates may also be supplied as system credentials named keyring-setup.dm-verity.NAME, keyring-setup.fs-verity.NAME or keyring-setup.bpf.NAME, each holding one PEM encoded certificate. Following the specification's advice for verifiers retrieved from elsewhere, they are placed into the ephemeral load path as /run/voa/OS/ROLE/default/x509/NAME-certificate.pem before the hierarchy is searched, so that masking and merging apply to them like to any other file. With --dry-run they are only reported and not placed, hence they do not appear among the certificates shown. The credential keyring-setup.os may hold a whitespace separated list of OS identifiers to look up instead of the ones derived from os-release, e.g. for a generic initrd. Credentials are the way to hand a trust anchor to an initrd without rebuilding it; they are as trustworthy as the mechanism that delivered them. See systemd.system-credentials7.

refsect1.title: Options

listitem.para: Look up the VOA hierarchy and os-release below the specified directory instead of the root of the running system. The keyrings are always those of the running kernel.
Look up the specified VOA OS identifier instead of the ones derived from os-release. May be used multiple times.

Look up the specified VOA context instead of default. May be used multiple times. Note that kernel keyrings cannot distinguish contexts: every certificate enrolled is trusted for all uses of the keyring.

Controls whether the keyrings are sealed and locked down after enrollment. Takes auto (the default, see above), yes to seal every keyring found, or no to only enroll. Note that with no the enrolled set provides no guarantee whatsoever, as any privileged process may change it later.

Show which certificates would be enrolled into which keyring, and the current state of the keyrings, without changing anything. Note that whether a keyring is sealed cannot be determined without changing it, only whether it was locked down, and that the number of keys in a locked down keyring is only shown by /proc/keys.

refsect1.para: If one or more KEYRING names are passed, only those keyrings are processed.

refsect1.title: Exit status
refsect1.para: On success, 0 is returned. This includes the cases where a keyring does not exist, was sealed by the kernel at boot, or was provisioned by an earlier boot stage already. If a configured certificate could not be enrolled because of its contents, EX_DATAERR (65) is returned. If the kernel refused an operation, 1 is returned. Enrollment failures never prevent the keyring from being sealed: an unsealed keyring is not consulted by the kernel, an unlocked one may be emptied by anyone, and a sealed subset of the configured certificates is preferable to either.

listitem.para: Kernel parameters leaving the respective keyring open for provisioning at boot. Without them the kernel seals the keyring empty and nothing can be enrolled. Note that bpf.keyring_unsealed=1 also makes the kernel refuse caller-supplied keyrings for the verification of BPF program signatures for the whole boot, whether or not provisioning succeeded. See the kernel documentation for details.

refsect1.title: Security Considerations
refsect1.para: The trust the kernel puts into the enrolled certificates is only as strong as the trust in the files they were read from. Provisioning from the initrd of a signed Unified Kernel Image is the intended deployment. Provisioning on the host system after the initrd, or on systems without an initrd, happens after other privileged code had the opportunity to add keys to the still open keyrings.

Until the keyring is sealed and locked down, any privileged process may add keys to it or remove keys from it, and a certificate with the same subject and key identifier as an enrolled one replaces it. Privileged containers sharing the initial user namespace are no exception. Once locked down, keys cannot be added or removed anymore until the next boot: a compromised certificate is revoked by masking it in the VOA hierarchy and rebooting. Note that a soft reboot does not reset the keyrings, and that with a modular dm-verity the .dm-verity keyring is recreated whenever the module is reloaded.
Certificate validity periods are not enforced by the kernel. Signatures continue to be verified against the kernel's revocation list.
